claims.feature: other: the inevitable left off the page
claims.claim: Katherine Olley says that once events become inevitable Kay largely leaves them to be supplied by the imagination of the reader.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Guy Gavriel Kay: A Short Introduction', University of Oxford Podcasts video lecture, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: he largely leaves them to be supplied by the imagination

claims.claim: Olley names the retrospective construction of history and its many ironies as one of Kay's chief thematic concerns across all his works.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, University of Oxford Podcasts, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: The nature of history is retrospective construction

claims.claim: Olley says Kay's books are so closely inspired by real events that he sometimes seems not to rewrite history but to write around it.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, University of Oxford Podcasts, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: not to rewrite history but to write around it

claims.claim: Olley attributes Kay's unique style and tone to his ability to find power in quiet moments as well as in brash heroic or sweeping romantic ones.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, University of Oxford Podcasts, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: ability to find power in these quiet moments

claims.claim: Olley says the verse lament that closes The Lions of Al-Rassan heightens the pathos of the moment and lets Kay impart a sense of closure.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', 16 December 2020
claims.quote: heightens the pathos of the moment

claims.claim: Allard argues that in A Song for Arbonne songs and poetry are not prophetic, unlike in Middle-earth, and act only as a cue for action rather than causing events.
claims.source: James Allard, University of Waterloo, 1997, hosted at BrightWeavings
claims.quote: nevertheless acts only as a cue for action

claims.claim: Ringel notes that magic in Arbonne is confined to small things, the coinage of hearth and heart, in keeping with the small amount of pagan marvel in real medieval romances.
claims.quote: Confined to small things, the coinage of hearth and heart

claims.claim: The commenter newtothegarden characterises Kay's position as a compassion that is deeper because of the terribleness of what people do.
claims.source: u/newtothegarden, r/Fantasy thread 'Some thoughts about Tigana (heavy spoilers)'
claims.quote: compassion that is deeper because of the terribleness

claims.claim: Tarantino describes the pervading tone of Kay's writing as elegiac and quietly valedictory.
claims.quote: suffused with an elegiac tone and the gentle melancholy of farewells
claims.page: body, paragraph beginning 'These are novels about the importance'

claims.claim: Tarantino contrasts Kay's delivery with bombast, calling the stories meditative instead.
claims.quote: They are meditative rather than bombastic.

claims.claim: Loutfi reports that she personally finds Kay's prose annoying, placing herself among readers who dislike it.
claims.quote: many other readers find it to be annoying
claims.page: lesson 3, 'Beautiful Prose is a double-edged Sword'

claims.claim: Kay lists 'No sentence fragments' and 'One narrator only' among writing rules he says he has broken.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'The First Rule of Write Club Is...', Literary Hub, 6 July 2016
claims.quote: No sentence fragments. One narrator only. (Yes, I’ve broken all of these.)
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'But there might be harm'

claims.claim: Kay argues that the notion that art has rules to be followed may itself do harm.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Literary Hub, 6 July 2016
claims.quote: there might be harm in the very notion that there are rules
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'But there might be harm'

claims.claim: Kay separates the rules of commercial success from the rules of writing as well as one can.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Literary Hub, 6 July 2016
claims.quote: The rules of smart commerce are not identical to the rules
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'And there is nothing wrong with it'

claims.claim: Snyder attributes the sensual, vivid language of Under Heaven to the influence of the T'ang poets.
claims.quote: as though ever mindful of the inspirational influence of the T’ang poets

verdicts.trueWording: Once events become inevitable, he largely leaves them to be supplied by the imagination of the reader.
verdicts.note: Live page carries no inline transcript; the official .srt subtitle file linked from the page (media.podcasts.ox.ac.uk/engfac/fantasy_lit/introduction-guy-gavriel-kaydefault.srt) was fetched raw and flattened. Quote present word for word, in the Under Heaven section, immediately after the epilogue discussion. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: The nature of history is retrospective construction, and its many ironies is one of his chief thematic concerns across all of his works.
verdicts.note: Raw .srt transcript. Quote verbatim; the sentence continues exactly as the claim states (many ironies, chief thematic concerns, across all his works). The page's own blurb independently corroborates: 'his reflections on the retrospective construction of history'.

verdicts.trueWording: so closely inspired by real world events that he sometimes seems not to rewrite history but to write around it
verdicts.note: Raw .srt transcript: 'Indeed, so well researched a casebooks [ASR garble of "are Kay's books"] and so closely inspired by real world events that he sometimes seems not to rewrite history but to write around it.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Kay's ability to find power in these quiet moments, as well as ... the brash, heroic moments or the sweeping romantic moments ... gives his work a really unique style and tone.
verdicts.note: Raw .srt transcript, after the mosaicist/iconoclasm passage. Quote verbatim, and all three limbs (quiet moments, brash heroic and sweeping romantic moments, unique style and tone) are in the same sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: Breaking into poetry here heightens the pathos of the moment ... and it allows Kay to impart a sense of closure.
verdicts.note: Raw .srt of the companion lecture 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature' (verse-and-prose-fantasy-literaturedefault.srt). Quote verbatim, and 'allows Kay to impart a sense of closure' follows in the same sentence. The auto-caption garbles the title ('The Lions of Other Ascend', 'our Rassam') but the verse she reads is Al-Rassan's closing lament ('the ending of our Rassam, the beloved'), so the title limb is unambiguous.

verdicts.trueWording: songs and poetry are not prophetic ... unlike Middle Earth ... nevertheless acts only as a cue for action
verdicts.note: brightweavings.com/legislatorsarbonne/ fetched raw (HTTP 200). Header confirms 'an undergraduate paper by James Allard written when he was at the University of Waterloo... presented at the 1997 Academic Conference of Canadian Science Fiction and Fantasy.' Quote verbatim in the opening argument; the 'cue for action' clause is grammatically about 'language', which in context is the songs and poetry of Arbonne, and the sentence ends 'providing direction for action, but never supplying the action itself.'

verdicts.trueWording: magic in Arbonne was ... Confined to small things, the coinage of hearth and heart
verdicts.note: brightweavings.com/kaysprovence/ fetched raw. Byline confirms Faye Ringel, Ph.D., versions presented March 2009 and August 2009. Quote verbatim; Ringel quotes Beatritz's line and frames it 'in keeping with the relatively small amount of "merveilleux paien" [pagan miracles or marvels] ... in the real Medieval romances', supporting the pagan-marvel limb.

verdicts.trueWording: Kay's position often seems to me to be compassion that is deeper because of the terribleness.
verdicts.note: Live reddit.com returned HTTP 403 (both .json and old.reddit interstitial), so recovered via the Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20250304145029id_/... . Quote verbatim; the page's JSON-LD attributes the comment to author name 'newtothegarden' (t2_doybtw0f, t1_jwnbsp8, 2023-08-17), and the next sentence ('Humans do terrible things because we're human') supports the 'of what people do' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: Kay's writings are suffused with an elegiac tone and the gentle melancholy of farewells.
verdicts.note: c2cjournal.ca fetched raw (HTTP 200); JSON-LD confirms author Bob Tarantino, datePublished 2016-09-07. Quote verbatim in the paragraph beginning 'These are novels about the importance and impacts of history', exactly as cited. 'Pervading' maps to 'suffused with' and 'quietly valedictory' to 'the gentle melancholy of farewells'.

verdicts.trueWording: They are meditative rather than bombastic.
verdicts.note: Same raw c2cjournal.ca fetch, closing section as cited: 'Guy Gavriel Kay tells stories which are true... They are meditative rather than bombastic.' Quote verbatim including the full stop; both limbs (contrast with bombast, stories called meditative) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: many other readers find it to be annoying. I am in the latter camp!
verdicts.note: metastellar.com fetched raw (HTTP 200); byline Amira Loutfi present. Under the cited heading '3. Beautiful Prose is a double-edged Sword': 'many people love Kay's prose, but many other readers find it to be annoying. I am in the latter camp!' Quote verbatim, and 'I am in the latter camp' supplies the personal-dislike limb.

verdicts.trueWording: No sentence fragments. One narrator only. (Yes, I've broken all of these.)
verdicts.note: lithub.com fetched raw (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim, curly apostrophe included, in the paragraph beginning 'But there might be harm', within the list 'Never revise until you are done with the book. Never use a prologue. Short chapters. No sentence fragments. One narrator only.' Both named rules and the broken-them-all limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: But there might be harm in the very notion that there are rules to be followed in art.
verdicts.note: Same raw lithub fetch, opening the cited paragraph. Quote verbatim; the sentence completes with 'to be followed in art', supplying the art limb of the claim.

verdicts.trueWording: The rules of smart commerce are not identical to the rules of good writing.
verdicts.note: Same raw lithub fetch, in the paragraph beginning 'And there is nothing wrong with it, at all' as cited. Quote verbatim; the preceding sentence, 'this is still not the same thing as writing as best one can', supports the claim's 'writing as well as one can' phrasing.

verdicts.trueWording: the language - as though ever mindful of the inspirational influence of the T'ang poets - is sensual and vivid
verdicts.note: brightweavings.com/review-by-novelist-midori-snyder/ fetched raw (HTTP 200); header confirms 'Review by novelist Midori Snyder' of Under Heaven, reproduced with permission. Quote verbatim (curly apostrophe in T'ang) in the final paragraphs; 'is sensual and vivid' closes the same sentence.
